steps.title: Steep slopes
steps.body: The Mosel has some of the steepest vineyards in the world. The Bremmer Calmont, in the Lower Mosel, reaches about 65 degrees, often called Europe's steepest. Vines are trained on single poles, Einzelpfahl, and work is by hand, sometimes with monorails. Steepness gives more sun and drainage, but costs are high.

steps.title: Slate
steps.body: Most top vineyards are on Devonian slate, grey, blue or red. Slate drains well, absorbs heat by day and releases it at night, helping ripening. Broken slate on the surface reflects light. Many link slate to the Mosel's mineral, smoky character, though the science is debated; its effect on heat and drainage is clear.
steps.highlight: Slate stores heat and drains well

steps.prompt: How does slate help Mosel vineyards?
options: It absorbs and releases heat and drains well
It holds water like a sponge
steps.explanation: Heat storage and drainage help ripening.

steps.title: Famous sites
steps.body: Famous vineyards include Wehlener Sonnenuhr, with its sundial; Bernkasteler Doctor, among Germany's most expensive; Ürziger Würzgarten, on red slate; Graacher Himmelreich; and Piesporter Goldtröpfchen. Labels name the village plus the vineyard, like Wehlener Sonnenuhr, from Wehlen.

steps.explanation: Clos de Vougeot is in Burgundy.
